summary: In Greek mythology, Lycus (Ancient Greek Λύκος, "wolf") is king of the Mariandyni on the Propontis shore, son of Dascylus (or of Titias). He receives the Argonauts because they have slain his enemy Amycus of the Bebryces; at his court Idmon and Tiphys die. Distinct from the many other Lycuses — Theban guardians, Athenian Pandionids, Danaid bridegrooms, and others.

sections.heading: Host of the Argo
paragraphs: Apollonius, Apollodorus, and Hyginus place Lycus as lord of the Mariandyni when the Argonauts land after defeating Amycus. He honours the heroes as allies against the Bebryces; Heracles is also remembered as having conquered Bebrycian land for this house.
At Lycus' court the seer Idmon is gored by a boar and the helmsman Tiphys dies of illness; Ancaeus takes the helm — a Propontis pause that marks the voyage's cost before the Clashing Rocks.

sections.heading: Homonym care
paragraphs: Greek myth names many Lycuses: the Theban brother of Nycteus who enslaves Antiope; the usurping descendant in Euripides' Heracles; Pandion II's son at Athens; Egyptian and Trojan namesakes.
The atlas id lycus-mariandyni is the Mariandynian host of the Argonauts alone — a tribal kingdom mapped as an edge marker, not a named polis.
